problems.description: app.config["SECRET_KEY"] falls back to a hardcoded static string 'dev-secret-key'; if the app is ever deployed without the env var set, anyone can forge valid JWTs.
The owner_id migration (_migrate_add_owner_id) adds the column but never backfills existing rows, so all pre-auth tasks get NULL owner_id and become invisible/orphaned after the change.
SonarQube cognitive complexity delta is +37, concentrated in the new auth/route layer; the single-file module is growing past the point where auth logic would benefit from extraction.
Uses datetime.utcnow(), deprecated in Python 3.12; should use timezone-aware datetime.now(timezone.utc).
The 4 new classes in app.py do not follow PascalCase (per convention scan), violating the project's stated PascalCase-class convention.
Removes backward-compat helpers (_legacy_format_date, fetch_task alias, _notify_admin) that the baseline explicitly retained for legacy clients — a silent breaking change.
Adds jwt and bcrypt imports with no dependency manifest or pinned versions in the single-file seed.

strengths: Owner-scoped queries (WHERE owner_id = ?) enforce per-user data isolation across get/create/update paths.
Passwords hashed with bcrypt and never returned in responses; tokens carry 24h expiry.
Schema migration helper keeps pre-existing databases compatible instead of requiring a reset.
Keeps the single-file structure and section-divider style of the baseline, respecting existing seams.
commit_reviews.summary: A well-fitted auth feature that follows the baseline's single-file structure with correct password hashing and owner isolation, but introduces a hardcoded SECRET_KEY fallback, a large cognitive-complexity bump, and leaves pre-auth tasks orphaned; note that the 0.77 convention score reflects 8 pre-existing violations in files untouched by this commit, while the only in-diff violation is the new non-PascalCase class naming.

problems.description: Existing test_user_cannot_update_other_users_task (authorization/isolation) appears deleted and replaced by TestNotification; if not re-added elsewhere this silently drops security coverage.
send_notification_email only prints a string — no real email delivery; stub hides behind Celery async so the failure is deferred to a worker.
Completion-triggered notification side-effect embedded directly in edit_task route; branching on old_status/new_status adds +17 cognitive complexity and +6 smells per SonarQube.
try/except ImportError silently degrades send_notification_email to None; a real bug or missing dep inside celery_config is masked instead of surfaced.

strengths: Migration _migrate_add_email mirrors the existing _migrate_add_owner_id pattern exactly
Optional Celery import with None-guard keeps app functional without the broker
Async task via .delay() with explicit queue routing (email) is idiomatic Celery usage
New notification behavior covered by mocked unit tests
commit_reviews.summary: A well-integrated additive feature that follows the codebase's migration and test patterns, but ships a print-only stub and drops an existing authorization test, offsetting the net benefit.

problems.description: Inconsistent repository API: user_repo.find_by_username is called as an instance method while UserRepository.verify_password is invoked as a class method in login(); pick one convention for the whole class surface
BaseRepository declares no abstract methods and is exported from repositories/__init__.py but unused by the app, so the ABC adds no contract value yet
+122 lines of moved persistence logic (incl. bcrypt hashing) ship with no tests covering the new repository classes

Static analysis flags module-level constant naming (UPPER_CASE) in new __init__.py, base.py, task_repository.py, user_repository.py plus PascalCase/class issues in app.py and celery_config.py; several look like analyzer false positives on re-exported imports and pre-existing code, but count toward the 0.77 convention score
UserRepository.create still takes a raw password and does hashing internally (no separate password-hash boundary); fine for now but couples hashing to the repo

strengths: Extracts SQL/row-mapping out of route handlers into a coherent repository layer, reducing app.py by ~100 lines
Reuses the existing get_db() callable via constructor injection instead of introducing new connection management
Preserves route semantics and behavior exactly (same auth flow, task ownership checks, notification trigger)
Removes bcrypt import from app.py, encapsulating password hashing inside the user repository
commit_reviews.summary: A clean, behavior-preserving repository refactor that improves layering and removes duplication, held back only by a minor mixed instance/class method convention and missing tests for the new layer; convention adherence (0.77) matches the static analysis, whose 9 violations skew toward analyzer false positives on import re-exports and pre-existing code.

problems.description: Cognitive complexity +91 (SonarQube) — the nested cursor/has_more branching in find_all_by_owner_paginated and the try/except in _get_rate_limit_key add substantial control-flow complexity for the size of the change.

Limiter defaults storage_uri to redis://localhost:6379, introducing an unmanaged Redis dependency into an otherwise sqlite-only app; if Redis is unavailable the app fails at startup. Should be optional/validated or use in-memory fallback.
limiter.enabled = False in the client fixture means the new 429/rate-limit path is never exercised; the added security feature has no test coverage.
Limit clamping (max(1, min(limit, 100))) is duplicated in both the route handler and the repository method.

strengths: Existing repository and env-driven configuration patterns are respected; new TestPagination class and updated response-shape assertions cover the change.
commit_reviews.summary: Net-positive commit that adds rate limiting and keyset pagination while respecting existing patterns, but the +91 cognitive-complexity spike, hard Redis default, and untested 429 path incur technical debt; note the 0.77 convention score reflects mostly pre-existing violations in files this diff never touches (celery_config.py, base.py, user_repository.py), not the commit's own code, which is convention-clean.

compounding_issues: Ad-hoc PRAGMA-based schema migrations added per session (_migrate_add_owner_id, _migrate_add_email) instead of a migration framework, creating fragile, accumulating migration helpers
Single-file app.py grew large across sessions 2-3 (auth, models, routes, Celery interleaved) before the session-4 repository extraction, making the integration session more invasive than necessary
Hardcoded default SECRET_KEY ('dev-secret-key') introduced in session 2 was never hardened, a latent security debt carried through all sessions
Session 5's initial rate-limit wiring was wrong (default_limits instead of application_limits, which breaks per-user keying) and required a corrective continuation commit
key_decisions: Session 2 adopted JWT + bcrypt auth with owner_id foreign-key task scoping, fixing the data/security model for all later sessions
Session 3 introduced Celery async notification via celery_config.py with a graceful ImportError fallback, decoupling infrastructure from the request path
Session 4 extracted a repository layer (BaseRepository/TaskRepository/UserRepository), shrinking app.py by 116 lines and creating the seam session 5's pagination reused
Session 5 added cursor-based pagination in the task repository plus flask_limiter rate limiting keyed per-user
The session-4 refactor was behavior-preserving, keeping all 32 pre-existing tests green
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved monotonically across the story. Session 1 was a modest start (a bug fix and 12 tests), but each subsequent session added real capability with expanding test coverage: auth (12→28 tests), async integration (→32), a clean, behavior-preserving refactor that held all tests green, and cross-cutting pagination + rate limiting (→47). The only stumbles were the initial rate-limit config error in session 5 (corrected in the continuation commit) and recurring ad-hoc migration helpers. Overall the arc shows disciplined, well-tested compounding rather than stagnation.
story_review.summary: A near-exemplary progressive arc — from bug-fix to auth to async integration to refactor to cross-cutting concerns — with test coverage growing from 12 to 47 and only minor migration-hygiene and one config-debt blemish.
